sec.title: Background
sec.p: Sepsis remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in neonatal and pediatric intensive care units (NICU/PICU). Given the rapid clinical deterioration of these vulnerable populations, shifting from reactive diagnosis to proactive prediction of sepsis onset is crucial. Multidimensional hematological parameters may provide new insights for risk stratification. While routine complete blood count (CBC) is widely used, the predictive potential of high-dimensional hematological cell morphology features that extend beyond traditional CBC remains under-investigated in large-scale pediatric cohorts.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This multicenter study utilized a large-scale dataset from the CALM2302 project, encompassing 17,066 critically ill neonates and children across 30 Chinese hospitals between October 2020 and October 2023. We developed population-specific CatBoost models for NICU and PICU to predict sepsis onset. To mitigate class imbalance, random undersampling was applied to the training sets. From a candidate pool of 1,924 parameters (37 routine CBC and 1,887 research features), optimized signatures of approximately 200 features were selected for each population. Model performance was evaluated by the area under the ROC curve (AUC) across internal and dual external validation cohorts. Furthermore, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was performed to ensure model interpretability and identify key biological predictors.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among the total cohort, 10,347 infants were categorized into the NICU cohort (sepsis incidence: 7.48%), while 6,719 children formed the PICU cohort (sepsis incidence: 10.92%). CatBoost was identified as the optimal architecture after benchmarking nine machine learning algorithms. The population-specific simplified 18-variable models demonstrated robust performance. In the NICU cohort, the model achieved an internal AUC of 0.846 and external AUCs of 0.742 and 0.827. For the PICU cohort, corresponding AUCs were 0.803, 0.717, and 0.811. These simplified models maintained highly comparable discriminative power to the full models (range of AUC attenuation: 0.005–0.027). SHAP analysis identified 18 key predictive features for each cohort, with only two shared features between the two populations and the remaining being cohort-specific. Notably, most of these 18 features were research parameters rather than traditional blood counts indices. Furthermore, most of these features remained statistically significant in multivariable analyses after adjustment for age, sex, and study sites.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this large multicenter cohort, we developed and validated simplified 18-variable models that accurately predict sepsis in both neonatal and pediatric populations. By capturing early hematological morphological alterations beyond traditional blood counts, these models offer a robust, interpretable, and clinically accessible solution for proactive sepsis management in intensive care units.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sepsis remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in neonatal and pediatric intensive care units (NICUs and PICUs) [1–4]. Globally, approximately 3 million neonates and 1.2 million children develop sepsis each year, with case fatality rates reaching up to 50% in neonates and 4%−50% in children [5–7]. Without prompt recognition and treatment, sepsis may rapidly progress to multi-organ dysfunction and death [8–11].

Despite advances in diagnostic definitions, early identification of children at risk for sepsis remains challenging. The recently proposed Phoenix Sepsis Criteria (PSC) define infection-associated life-threatening organ dysfunction but are not intended to predict sepsis onset [12, 13]. Blood culture remains the gold standard for confirming bacteremia in suspected sepsis, yet it is hampered by unsatisfactory sensitivity. Preceding antibiotic administration, insufficient blood sampling volume and low circulating bacterial load frequently lead to false-negative results, with turnaround time extending up to 48 h [14, 15]. Conventional biomarkers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), are widely used but demonstrate suboptimal sensitivity and specificity during early infection [16, 17]. Pediatric and neonatal scoring systems (e.g., PRISM, PIM, SNAP, SNAP-II, SNAPPE-II) primarily estimate mortality risk rather than predict early sepsis [18–21]. Collectively, these limitations highlight an unmet clinical need for readily available, low-cost predictive indicators derived from routine laboratory testing.

Modern automated hematology analyzers equipped with flow imaging generate standard routine complete blood count (CBC) items including white blood cell (WBC), red blood cell (RBC) and platelet (PLT) [22–24], alongside numerous additional morphometric and biophysical cellular parameters. Owing to the direct linkage between cellular phenotype and systemic inflammation, these parameters capture early hematopoietic changes triggered by subclinical inflammation long before overt sepsis manifestations emerge, thereby offering a biological basis for early sepsis prediction. Despite this promising diagnostic potential, such multidimensional hematologic markers remain understudied in neonatal and pediatric sepsis research, mainly due to technical hurdles for feature extraction and poor clinical recognition of these hidden indicators. Given the high dimensionality and intercorrelation of these parameters, machine learning provides a feasible strategy to synthesize multiple indicators and circumvent the deficiencies of single-biomarker-based diagnosis

This study therefore aims to explore and validate the early predictive performance of these underutilized CBC-derived morphometric parameters for sepsis in critically ill neonates and children using machine learning models.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This multicenter retrospective study was conducted under the Chinese Association for Laboratory Medicine (CALM2302) project, including critically ill neonates and children admitted to NICUs and PICUs across 30 hospitals in 12 provinces and 23 cities in China from October 2020 to October 2023. The study followed TRIPOD-AI guidance [25], with independent ethical approval obtained from all participating medical centers; the central coordinating ethics approval was issued by the Ethics Review Committee of Zhujiang Hospital, Southern Medical University (Approval No. 2023-KY-054-01). This study was pre-registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06034639, registration date: 2023-08-11). Conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki [26], this study obtained Ethics Committee (EC) approval for waiving individual written informed consent due to its retrospective nature. All data were anonymized to ensure no identification of individual participants, and the waiver did not compromise participants’ rights and interests. An overview of the study design is presented in Fig. 1.

caption.p: Overview of the study workflow. NICU neonatal intensive care unit, PICU pediatric intensive care unit, CatBoost categorical boosting, RF random forest, SVM support vector machine, LightGBM light gradient boosting machine, KNN k-nearest neighbors, RPART recursive partitioning and regression trees, XGBoost extreme gradient boosting, NB naïve Bayes, FNNs feedforward neural networks, AUC area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, SHAP SHapley Additive exPlanations

sec.p: All patients younger than 18 years admitted to NICUs and PICUs were considered. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) sepsis at admission, (2) absence or unavailability of CBC testing data prior to sepsis onset, (3) incomplete clinical records, (4) known chromosomal abnormalities, or (5) pregnancy. After applying these criteria, the development cohort comprised 11,798 patients (7,595 NICU; 4,203 PICU). External validation cohorts 1 and 2 included 1,949 (1,221 NICU; 728 PICU) and 3,666 (1,650 NICU; 2,016 PICU) patients, respectively. Separate prediction models were developed for NICU and PICU populations to account for physiological and clinical differences between neonates and older children.

sec.title: Outcome
sec.p: The primary endpoint was new-onset in-hospital sepsis developing after admission among initially non-septic critically ill children and neonates. In line with predefined exclusion criteria, subjects diagnosed with sepsis upon admission were entirely excluded at enrollment and hence not followed for outcome analysis (i.e., these patients were censored from the cohort by exclusion rather than during follow-up). Sepsis events were ascertained based on final discharge diagnoses coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) [27]. Owing to limitations of retrospective administrative data, exact timestamps of sepsis onset were unavailable.

sec.title: Multidimensional hematological parameters
sec.p: Routine CBC testing on automated hematology analyzers (BC-6000PLUS, BC-6800PLUS, and BC-7500; Mindray Bio-Medical Electronics Co., Ltd) provides standard CBC indices and generates underlying cellular scatter plots and fluorescence images as part of the measurement process [28, 29]. While only the routine indices are reported clinically, the raw image and signal outputs contain substantially richer morphological information. Using a proprietary image-based feature extraction algorithm, we quantified detailed morphology- and distribution-related characteristics from these analyzer-generated images. These derived parameters included measures of central tendency, dispersion, skewness, kurtosis, population boundaries, projection areas, and variability. In total, 1,924 multidimensional features were obtained, comprising 37 routine CBC parameters and 1,887 image-derived research parameters. Definitions are provided in eTable 1, and the feature-extraction workflow is illustrated in eFigure 1.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data preprocessing and feature selection. Data preprocessing and selection were performed separately for the NICU and PICU datasets. Variables with > 5% missing values or near-zero variance were excluded. Highly correlated features were filtered in two sequential steps: (1) for all image-derived research parameters, we retained only one feature from each pair with a Spearman correlation coefficient > 0.8; (2) using the remaining research-derived features obtained after Step 1, we assessed pairwise correlations between these retained research features and standard CBC parameters. Any pair with correlation > 0.8 was processed by discarding the research-derived feature and preserving the corresponding CBC parameter [30, 31]. After this procedure, 203 and 204 features were retained for NICU and PICU cohorts, respectively.

Data splitting and resampling. The development cohort was randomly split into training (70%) and internal test (30%) sets, preserving NICU/PICU ratios. To address class imbalance, a 1:1 random undersampling was applied to the training set, while the internal test set remained in its original distribution [32, 33]. All random procedures used a fixed seed for reproducibility.

Model development and evaluation. Classification models were trained using the mlr3 package (version 0.22.1) in R (version 4.3.2). Nine algorithms were evaluated: random forest (RF), light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), categorical boosting (CatBoost), support vector machine (SVM), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), naïve Bayes (NB), recursive partitioning and regression trees (RPART), and feedforward neural networks (FNNs). Each model underwent five-fold cross-validation on the balanced training set, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was used to compare performance. The best-performing model was further optimized with five-fold cross-validation and random search for hyperparameter tuning. Performance was evaluated on the internal test set and two external validation cohorts.

Model interpretation and feature prioritization. Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) [34], a game theoretic approach, was used to quantify feature attributions. Features were ranked by their mean absolute SHAP values. A sequential forward selection added features iteratively in descending importance [35], recording cumulative AUC via five-fold cross-validation. Selection stopped when no further improvement was observed, retaining the top predictors for interpretation and visualization.

Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses of selected predictors. After SHAP value ranking and sequential forward feature selection, we obtained the final panel of candidate predictors. First, crude univariable logistic regression was performed to examine the association between each retained parameter and sepsis outcome. Second, covariate-adjusted single-predictor logistic regression models were constructed for every predictor, with age, sex and study center incorporated as predefined confounding covariates. Effect sizes were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The false discovery rate (FDR) correction via the Benjamini-Hochberg method was applied separately to P-values from crude univariable and covariate-adjusted univariable regression analyses to mitigate type I error inflation from multiple comparisons.

Descriptive statistics. Continuous variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range, IQR), as appropriate. Categorical variables were presented as count (%). Statistical significance was defined as two-sided P-value < 0.05. For multiple comparisons, P-value were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method to control FDR, and an FDR-adjusted P-value (P-FDR) < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Baseline characteristics of the study cohorts
sec.p: The study included one development cohort and two external validation cohorts from NICU and PICU populations (Table 1). In the NICU, the development cohort comprised 7,538 neonates, with validation cohorts 1 and 2 including 1,206 and 1,603 patients, respectively. The median age ranged from 0.00 to 0.01 days (interquartile ranges [IQRs], 0.00–0.00 to 0.00–0.02) across the three cohorts. The proportion of female patients ranged from 39.9% to 43.4%, and median hospital stay ranged from 7 to 10 days. The incidence of sepsis in the NICU cohorts was 6.9–9.5%. In the PICU, the development cohort comprised 4,036 patients, while validation cohorts 1 and 2 included 709 and 1,974 patients, respectively. The median age ranged from 1.65 to 2.65 years (IQRs 0.13–6.00 to 0.42–7.50) across the three cohorts. The proportion of female patients ranged from 38.2% to 42.5%, and median hospital stay ranged from 10 to 11 days. The incidence of sepsis in the PICU cohorts varied from 10.3% to 12.5%. We further summarized blood culture profiles of all enrolled patients in eTable 2. The overall positive rate of blood cultures was relatively low, and bacterial pathogens accounted for the vast majority of culture-confirmed infections.

caption.p: Baseline characteristics of patients in the development and external validation cohorts from NICU and PICU populations

sec.title: Performance comparison of machine learning algorithms
sec.p: Nine machine learning algorithms were evaluated for sepsis prediction using AUC as the primary metric, with analyses stratified by NICU and PICU populations (Fig. 2A, eTable 3). In NICU, CatBoost achieved the highest AUC (0.845), followed by RF (0.840) and LightGBM (0.839), while FNNs, RPART, and KNN performed less well (AUC < 0.75). In PICU, RF achieved the highest AUC (0.786), with CatBoost (0.782) and SVM (0.775) slightly lower. LightGBM and XGBoost showed moderate performance (AUCs 0.752 and 0.744), while FNNs, RPART, and KNN were less effective (AUC < 0.70). Considering overall performance and interpretability via SHAP analysis, CatBoost was selected for subsequent model development.

caption.p: Performance of machine learning models for sepsis prediction in NICU and PICU cohorts. (A) Comparison of AUC values across nine machine learning models in the NICU and PICU groups. (B-C) Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves of the CatBoost model in the NICU cohort (B) and the PICU cohort (C), evaluated in the training set, internal test set, and two external validation sets. (D) Cumulative AUC values as increasing numbers of hemocyte features were added according to importance ranking in the NICU and PICU cohorts. The vertical dashed line marks the point at which further addition of features yielded minimal incremental improvement (x = 18). (E-F) ROC curves of the feature-selected CatBoost model in the NICU cohort (E) and the PICU cohort (F), evaluated across the training set, internal test set, and external validation sets

sec.title: Construction and evaluation of the full CatBoost model
sec.p: The full CatBoost model was trained using five-fold cross-validation with random search for hyperparameter tuning. In the NICU internal test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.866, sensitivity 0.811, specificity 0.785, and overall accuracy 0.787. External validation cohorts 1 and 2 yielded AUCs of 0.769 and 0.840, respectively, indicating robust performance across independent cohorts. In the PICU internal test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.808, sensitivity 0.744, specificity 0.761, and overall accuracy 0.760. External cohorts 1 and 2 achieved AUCs of 0.736 and 0.827, respectively, demonstrating stable predictive performance. Overall, these results demonstrate that the CatBoost-based models reliably predict sepsis in both NICU and PICU patients and maintain strong performance when applied to independent external cohorts (Fig. 2B and C and eTable 4).

sec.title: Feature selection and validation of the reduced CatBoost model
sec.p: SHAP values from the full-feature CatBoost model were used to rank variables by mean absolute importance. Features were sequentially added according to importance, with incremental AUC recalculated at each step. Model performance increased rapidly with the top-ranked features and plateaued around the top 18 in both NICU and PICU populations, beyond which additional features contributed minimally (Fig. 2D). Based on this observation, a reduced CatBoost model was retrained using these top 18 features, with hyperparameters re-optimized via five-fold cross-validation and random search. The compact model achieved AUCs of 0.846, 0.742, and 0.827 in the internal test set and two external NICU cohorts, and 0.803, 0.717, and 0.811 in the corresponding PICU cohorts (Fig. 2E and F), only slightly lower than the full-feature models, indicating that the reduced model preserved strong predictive ability while markedly improving parsimony and interpretability.

sec.title: Identification and comparison of top predictive features across NICU and PICU populations
sec.p: SHAP-based feature importance analysis revealed distinct patterns between NICU and PICU cohorts (Fig. 3). The top predictive features in the NICU model encompassed indices derived from erythroid, granulocytic, lymphocytic, monocytic, and total leukocyte lineages, whereas the PICU model additionally included platelet-related parameters. Of these features, five in the NICU model [nucleated red blood cell percentage (NRBC%), hemoglobin concentration (HGB), immature granulocyte percentage (IMG%), mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), monocyte percentage (Mon%)] and five in the PICU model [plateletcrit (PCT), hematocrit (HCT), basophil percentage (Baso%), red blood cell count (RBC), HGB] were routine CBC parameters, while the remainder were hemogram-derived. Only two predictors, namely D_Ig_FSC_L0 (DIFF channel immature granulocyte particle cluster left boundary after removing 5% of particles on both sides in the forward scatter direction) and HGB, were shared between the two populations, indicating that the dominant discriminative features differed substantially between neonatal and pediatric sepsis (eFigure 2). Overall, these findings suggest that although both models rely on multidimensional hematologic information, the underlying cellular contributors to sepsis pr ediction vary markedly between NICU and PICU patients.

caption.p: SHAP-based feature importance and multivariable logistic regression analysis for the top hemocyte features in the NICU and PICU cohorts. (A) Top features contributing to sepsis prediction in the NICU cohort, ranked by mean absolute SHAP values (left). Corresponding adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from multivariable logistic regression are shown on the right. (B) Top predictors of sepsis in the PICU cohort, displayed using the same SHAP (left) and logistic regression (right) panels. Corresponding top predictors in the PICU cohort. Feature bars are color-coded by hematologic category (erythroid cells, granulocytes, lymphocytes, monocytes, total leukocytes, and platelets). The vertical red dashed line indicates OR = 1. ORs are displayed on a logarithmic scale

sec.title: Association and biological interpretation of top predictive features
sec.p: Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses confirmed that the top features from the reduced CatBoost models were independently associated with sepsis (eFig. 3, Figure 3).

In the NICU cohort, 14 of the 18 features were significantly associated with sepsis in univariable analysis (P < 0.05), and all remained significant after adjusting for sex, age, and study center. Several parameters reflecting enhanced nucleic acid fluorescence and increased heterogeneity of immune cells demonstrated strong associations with sepsis risk. Among these, D_Ig_SFL_Peak0 (DIFF channel immature granulocyte particle cluster peak position in the fluorescence direction) showed one of the largest effect sizes in the NICU cohort (adjusted OR 3.71, 95% CI 2.64–5.23), followed by D_Neu_SFL_W0 (DIFF channel neutrophil particle cluster left-right boundary width in the fluorescence direction without removing particles on both sides, adjusted OR 3.67, 95% CI 2.70–5.00), D_Mon_SFL_W9 (DIFF channel monocyte particle cluster left-right boundary width in the fluorescence direction after removing 14% of particles on both sides, adjusted OR 2.94, 95% CI 2.25–3.83), and N_Neu_SFL_L1 (WNB channel neutrophil particle cluster left boundary in the fluorescence direction after truncating at a height of 20 and removing 0.5% of particles on the left and 1% on the right, adjusted OR 2.78, 95% CI 2.20–3.52). Collectively, these parameters suggest increased nucleic acid content, immune-cell activation, and morphologic heterogeneity in neutrophils, immature granulocytes, and monocytes, supporting the presence of widespread immune dysregulation in septic neonates. All reported associations remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (all FDR-adjusted P < 0.001).

In the PICU cohort, 17 features were significant in univariable analysis, with 16 retaining significance in multivariable models. Several parameters reflecting aberrant fluorescence and scatter heterogeneity of peripheral leukocyte subpopulations were strongly associated with sepsis risk. Among these, D_Neu_SFL_W1 (DIFF channel neutrophil particle cluster left-right boundary width in the fluorescence direction after removing 1% of particles on both sides) exhibited the largest effect size (adjusted OR 3.14, 95% CI 2.20–4.49), followed by N_WBC_SFL_Kurt5 (WNB channel white blood cell particle cluster kurtosis in the fluorescence direction after truncating at a height of 50, adjusted OR 3.05, 95% CI 1.77–5.27), N_Neu_SSC_P15 (WNB channel neutrophil particle cluster centroid position in the side scatter direction after truncating at a height of 120, adjusted OR 2.38, 95% CI 1.82–3.11), D_Mon_SSC_W9 (DIFF channel monocyte particle cluster left-right boundary width in the side scatter direction after removing 14% of particles on both sides, adjusted OR 2.19, 95% CI 1.67–2.86), and N_Lym_SFL_W16 (WNB channel lymphocyte particle cluster left-right boundary width in the fluorescence direction after truncating at a height of 120 and removing 0.5% of particles on the left and 1% on the right, adjusted OR 2.13, 95% CI 1.69–2.68). These features collectively indicate increased nucleic acid variability and intracellular structural complexity of neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes, reflecting prominent leukocyte activation, morphological heterogeneity, and immune dysregulation among children with sepsis.

sec.title: Comparative predictive performance of the 18-feature model versus CBC and single-variable benchmark models
sec.p: We performed head-to-head comparisons of discriminative performance between the optimized 18-feature CatBoost model and the CBC model in NICU and PICU cohorts separately, with paired AUC differences evaluated by DeLong’s test and P values corrected via FDR multiple testing adjustment.

In the NICU cohort, the 18-feature model achieved higher AUCs than the CBC model in the training set, internal test set, and second external validation cohort, with ΔAUC values of 0.062, 0.033 and 0.032, respectively. The only exception was the first external validation cohort, where the CBC model showed a tiny AUC advantage (0.753 vs. 0.742, ΔAUC = − 0.011). Statistically significant improvement of the 18-feature model was only observed in the internal test set (p-adj = 0.045); no meaningful inter-model differences were identified in the two external validation cohorts (p-adj = 0.486 for external validation set 1, p-adj = 0.05 or external validation set 2) (Fig. 4A; Table 2).

caption.p: AUC comparison of the CBC model versus Top 18 feature model in NICU and PICU cohorts across one internal test set and two external validation datasets. (A) NICU cohort: pink bars = CBC model, light blue bars = Top 18 feature model. (B) PICU cohort: apricot bars = CBC model, light green bars = Top 18 feature model. DeLong’s tests were performed for inter-model AUC comparisons, and FDR-adjusted p-values (p.adj) are displayed above each paired bar
Comparative AUC values of the 18-feature CatBoost model and CBC model for NICU and PICU cohorts

table-wrap-foot.p: p-adj: FDR-adjusted P values derived from DeLong’s test for paired AUC comparisons

sec.p: For all four PICU datasets (training set, internal test set, two external validation cohorts), the 18-feature model numerically uniformly outperformed the CBC model, with ΔAUC ranging from 0.029 to 0.035 (0.035, 0.032, 0.029 and 0.032 sequentially) (Fig. 4B; Table 2). Statistical significance of the 18-feature model’s predictive gain was only attained in the second external validation cohort (p-adj = 0.015). Comparisons in the internal test set and first external validation cohort yielded non-significant adjusted P values of 0.118 and 0.245, respectively.

Beyond the CBC model, we further benchmarked the discriminative performance of the 18-feature CatBoost model against three single-variable baseline predictors, including white blood cell count (WBC), neutrophil count (Neu) and admission body temperature (eTable 5). Analyses for the temperature-only model excluded the second external validation cohort across both NICU and PICU groups, as temperature data were unavailable at this validation site. Across nearly all evaluable datasets, the three single-variable models yielded substantially lower AUC values relative to the 18-feature model, reflected by consistently positive ΔAUC values ranging from 0.026 to 0.277. Comparisons of WBC-only and Neu-only models produced statistically significant advantages for the 18-feature model in all test and external validation cohorts of both subgroups (all p-adj < 0.01, eFigure 4 A-4 F and eFigure 5 A-5 F). For temperature-based prediction, significant inter-model differences were only detected in the NICU internal test set (p-adj < 0.0001) and PICU internal test set (p-adj = 0.0005); no statistical superiority of the 18-feature model was observed in the first external validation cohort for either NICU (p-adj = 0.1907) or PICU (p-adj = 0.714) (eFigure 4G-4 H and eFigure 5G-5 H). Overall, single clinical indicators exhibited markedly weaker predictive discrimination than the 18-feature model.

Collectively, although the 18-feature CatBoost model only yielded modest numerical AUC improvements relative to the full 29-variable CBC panel across most cohorts and failed to reach statistical significance in several validation subsets, it achieved favorable discriminative capacity with substantially fewer predictive features. Meanwhile, the 18-feature model consistently outperformed all three single-variable baseline predictors, as integrating multiple hematological indicators enabled comprehensive capture of peripheral blood immune and inflammatory signatures that isolated individual markers cannot fully reflect.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this multicenter retrospective cohort study, we developed and externally validated two age-specific machine learning models based exclusively on multidimensional hematological parameters derived from routine complete blood count (CBC) testing to predict incident in-hospital sepsis among critically ill neonates and children who were free of sepsis at admission. Sepsis remains a life-threatening complication in critically ill neonates and pediatric patients because of its rapid progression, atypical early manifestations, high mortality, and delayed diagnosis using conventional clinical approaches. Reliable and readily implementable tools for early risk stratification remain limited. Against this backdrop, our study demonstrates that multidimensional hematological parameters obtained from routine CBC testing can provide effective early prediction of hospital-acquired sepsis without requiring additional laboratory tests or complex clinical variables.

Both the full and simplified CatBoost models demonstrated favorable discrimination across internal testing and two independent external validation cohorts. Notably, the compact 18-feature models maintained predictive performance comparable to, or slightly better than, the full 29-feature CBC models while substantially reducing model complexity. Furthermore, the CatBoost models consistently outperformed prediction models based on individual inflammatory indicators (white blood cell count, neutrophil count, and body temperature), highlighting the superiority of integrating multidimensional hematologic information over isolated biomarkers. Compared with previously reported prediction models, our approach achieved competitive predictive performance while relying solely on routinely available CBC-derived parameters, thereby enhancing feasibility for large-scale clinical implementation.

Among all evaluated algorithms, CatBoost consistently achieved the highest predictive performance in both NICU and PICU cohorts. As a gradient boosting decision tree algorithm, CatBoost effectively captures complex nonlinear interactions among heterogeneous hematologic variables while minimizing overfitting through ordered boosting. Its ability to automatically learn nonlinear relationships without extensive feature engineering makes it particularly suitable for high-dimensional clinical datasets [36]. In addition, SHAP analysis enabled transparent interpretation of feature contributions at the global level, improving model interpretability and facilitating potential clinical adoption.

A notable finding was that the hematologic signatures associated with incident sepsis differed substantially between critically ill neonates and older children. Logistic regression analyses further confirmed that the most influential multidimensional hematological parameters were independently associated with sepsis risk. In neonates, highly ranked predictors mainly reflected increased nucleic acid fluorescence and greater morphological heterogeneity of immature granulocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes, consistent with the unique immune immaturity and early cellular activation characteristic of neonatal infection. In contrast, pediatric patients exhibited predictive signatures dominated by alterations in scatter and fluorescence characteristics across multiple leukocyte subsets, reflecting the robust systemic inflammatory response typically observed during pediatric sepsis. These age-specific hematologic characteristics provide biological support for constructing separate predictive models rather than a unified model across all pediatric age groups.

The distinct hematologic signatures also have important implications for clinical implementation. In NICU patients, early hospital-acquired sepsis often presents with subtle and nonspecific manifestations because immune immaturity may blunt the inflammatory response. Since multidimensional hematological parameters are generated automatically during routine CBC testing, the NICU-specific prediction model could support dynamic risk stratification and identify high-risk infants who warrant closer monitoring or further clinical evaluation before overt clinical deterioration occurs. In PICU patients, systemic inflammatory responses may be more pronounced, although distinguishing sepsis-related changes from noninfectious critical illness remains challenging. The PICU-specific 18-feature model may serve as a rapid risk-stratification tool when routine CBC testing is performed during hospitalization, helping clinicians identify high-risk children who warrant closer clinical assessment and further microbiological or inflammatory testing. These differences underscore the need for population-specific implementation strategies tailored to the distinct pathophysiology, clinical presentations, and routine care pathways of NICUs and PICUs. Previous studies have primarily focused on conventional CBC indices, including white blood cell count [WBC], platelet count [PLT], red blood cell distribution width [RDW], and derived inflammatory ratios such as the immature-to-total neutrophil ratio [I: T ratio], neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio [NLR], platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio [PLR], and monocyte distribution width [MDW] [24, 31–43]. Although these biomarkers have demonstrated diagnostic or prognostic value, they may not fully capture the complex morphological and functional changes of circulating leukocytes during early sepsis. In contrast, all predictors included in our models were multidimensional hematological parameters extracted from scatter and fluorescence signals routinely generated during automated CBC analysis. Because these parameters require neither additional blood sampling nor supplementary laboratory testing, our models provide a cost-effective and easily scalable strategy for early sepsis screening.

Our study has several important strengths. First, unlike most previous studies that focused on diagnosing established sepsis, we specifically excluded patients with sepsis at admission and predicted incident in-hospital sepsis, addressing the clinically relevant objective of early risk identification. Second, the multicenter design with both internal and independent external validation substantially improves the robustness and generalizability of the proposed models compared with previous single-center studies. Third, the models rely exclusively on routinely available CBC-derived multidimensional hematological parameters without incorporating invasive laboratory tests, imaging findings, organ dysfunction markers, or complex clinical variables, thereby facilitating integration into routine clinical workflows.

Several limitations should also be acknowledged. First, the retrospective observational design is susceptible to incomplete data recording, selection bias, and residual confounding. In addition, sepsis was identified using discharge ICD-10 codes, and precise onset times were unavailable, preventing evaluation of fixed prediction windows and comparisons between early- and late-onset sepsis. Second, random downsampling was used during model training to address class imbalance, which may partly explain the reduced performance observed in external cohorts with real-world sepsis prevalence. Third, inconsistent data availability across participating centers precluded comparisons with established sepsis scoring systems, conventional inflammatory biomarkers such as procalcitonin and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and analyses according to microbiological etiology or blood culture positivity. Fourth, although multidimensional hematological parameters were extracted using dedicated software in the present study and thus cannot be directly acquired by conventional hematology analyzers at present, these variables are mathematically definable and could be incorporated directly into future hematology analyzer software to enable automated risk prediction during routine CBC testing. Finally, all participating centers were tertiary hospitals in China, and further prospective validation across different healthcare systems and ethnic populations is necessary to confirm generalizability. Moreover, although SHAP analysis improved model interpretability, the biological significance of several optical cytometric parameters remains incompletely understood and warrants further investigation through mechanistic studies integrating flow cytometry and multi-omics approaches.

Overall, our findings demonstrate that routinely available multidimensional hematological parameters contain substantial predictive information for incident hospital-acquired sepsis in critically ill neonates and children. The proposed age-specific CatBoost models provide accurate, interpretable, and clinically practical tools for early risk stratification and may facilitate timely recognition and intervention for sepsis in neonatal and pediatric intensive care settings.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In conclusion, this study demonstrates that multidimensional hematologic parameters carry strong and biologically meaningful signals for sepsis prediction in both neonatal and pediatric critical care populations. The integration of interpretable machine learning with routine hematologic data offers a transparent and clinically practical framework for precision risk assessment in pediatric sepsis.
